analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal agencies from finalizing any energy rule that could cut oil and gas production or raise gas prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote; it died after being referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered every federal agency to hold off on finalizing any new rule that would decrease domestic oil, gas, or biofuels production, raise gasoline prices, or in any way negatively affect domestic energy production, electricity generation, fuel transmission, infrastructure, or transportation fuels. The freeze would have lasted until the end of 2022 or until the national average gas price fell to $2.60 a gallon — whichever came first. Because almost any environmental, health, or safety rule touches energy production in some way, the bill amounts to a near-total pause on new energy regulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and biofuels producers gain the most: they would be shielded from any new federal rule that could slow production or add costs while fuel prices stay high. Drivers might see some relief at the pump if the industry passes along savings, but the bill guarantees none of it.

how_it_helps.text: It bars federal agencies from finalizing any rule that would decrease domestic oil, gas, or biofuels production or raise gasoline prices, giving producers a regulatory holiday while fuel prices are elevated.

It also blocks rules with any 'negative effects' on domestic energy production, electricity generation, transmission, infrastructure development, or transportation fuels — a broad standard that could cover many environmental, health, and safety rules.
The freeze runs until the earlier of January 1, 2023, or the day the national average gas price reaches $2.60 a gallon or less.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost through delayed environmental and health protections — cleaner air, safer infrastructure, and climate rules all wait — while the only benefit to consumers, lower gas prices, is indirect and not guaranteed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to delayed environmental protections

drawbacks.text: The trigger is written so broadly that nearly any new rule touching energy production could be blocked, including public health, safety, and environmental protections, not just rules that raise gas prices.
There is no mechanism requiring savings to reach consumers; the bill lowers industry costs first and leaves pump prices to the market.
The $2.60-a-gallon endpoint ties major policy decisions to a volatile world commodity price that Congress cannot control, making the freeze's duration unpredictable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers drivers only an indirect, uncertain hope of cheaper gas, while locking out a wide range of federal environmental and health rules for months. The costs fall broadly on the public; the benefits flow mainly to producers. On its own terms it is a poor trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on March 31, 2022, with Sen. Mike Braun and Sen. Steve Daines as cosponsors — three of 50 Senate Republicans.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and biofuels producers are no better off — the freeze never happened — but neither is anyone worse off. The public simply avoided the bill's broad regulatory pause, and no industry gained from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, by avoiding the regulatory freeze

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Mike Braun and Steve Daines

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or independent supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have shielded them from any new federal rule that could cut production or raise costs while prices were high. The savings would go to the industry first, while the public absorbed the delayed environmental and health protections.
The production-freeze language covers biofuels alongside oil and gas, so biofuel producers would have gotten the same regulatory holiday.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and fuel transmission companies
industries.note: Rules affecting electricity generation, transmission, and fuel infrastructure could also have been blocked, easing compliance costs. Consumers would still bear whatever those rules were meant to prevent.
